judgment.rationale: The conflict is real at the Win32 registration layer but is labeled too specifically. Current HotkeyConflictManager calls RegisterHotKey as a probe and treats ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED as a SystemConflict, even though that result can also mean another application registered the chord. The Settings UI then presents that category as a system shortcut and links generic Windows documentation. Because Color Picker uses its own activation path, the chord can still work while the probe reports an owner conflict.
evidence: The reporter reproduces the warning with Color Picker Win+Shift+C on Windows 11 build 26200 and confirms that Color Picker still opens.
Collaborator Jay-o-Way confirms that Win+Shift+C was historically assigned to Cortana/Charms but is generally deprecated on modern Windows 11.
Current HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey probes RegisterHotKey and returns true only for ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED.
The Win32 error does not identify whether Windows or another application owns the registration.
Current serialization places every such probe failure in sysConflicts, and Settings renders it as a system conflict.
Issue #50402 shows a separate conflict-attribution ambiguity and does not establish that Win+Shift+C itself is free.
Focused source review covered upstream main 71340eed47f7cf6f53b68b86a7939ad1240c3de7.
judgment.recommended_action: Approve a conflict-provenance design that preserves the warning but stops claiming every registration collision is a documented Windows shortcut.

fix_assessment.rationale: The current source proves the classification flaw: ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED is lossy owner evidence, yet the result is serialized as SystemConflict. The safe fix is to represent unknown external ownership honestly rather than suppress the collision.

proposed_fixes.title: Distinguish unknown external hotkey ownership from documented Windows shortcuts
proposed_fixes.root_cause: HotkeyConflictManager uses a temporary RegisterHotKey call as its only system-conflict probe. ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED proves that the chord is already registered, but not who owns it; the code stores that result in sysConflictHotkeyMap and the UI labels it as a system shortcut.
plan: Replace the boolean HasConflictWithSystemHotkey result with provenance that distinguishes a known in-app owner from an unknown external RegisterHotKey collision.
Serialize unknown external conflicts separately or with explicit provenance instead of sysConflicts/System.
Update Settings conflict text and links so unknown external ownership does not imply a documented Windows shortcut; preserve the warning and exact chord.
Add focused tests for successful probe registration, ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED, in-app conflicts, and self-conflict exclusion.
verification: Win+Shift+C on the affected Windows 11 build is shown as reserved by Windows or another application, not falsely asserted to be a documented system shortcut.
Known PowerToys-to-PowerToys conflicts still name both modules.
A free chord produces no warning, and a temporary successful registration is always unregistered.

confidence.rationale: The exact classification path is present in current source and directly explains both the warning and misleading documentation link; the fix can preserve safety without assuming the external owner.

issue_context.summary: Color Picker's working Win+Shift+C shortcut is reported as a system conflict on Windows 11. Current code can prove only that RegisterHotKey reports an existing registration, not that a documented Windows shortcut owns it.
known_information: The report uses PowerToys 0.101.2362 on Windows 11 build 26200.
Color Picker still activates with Win+Shift+C despite the warning.
The conflict UI links to a Windows shortcut list that does not document the chord for current Windows 11.
Win+Shift+C historically invoked Cortana or Charms on older Windows.
Current runner code classifies ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED as SystemConflict without identifying the owner.
Live upstream issue activity was reviewed through 2026-09-03T02:28:22Z.
inferences: Windows or another process may still reserve Win+Shift+C even though the public Windows 11 shortcut page does not list it.
The actionable defect is conflict provenance and wording, not necessarily the existence of a collision.
issue_context.analysis: Suppressing the warning would discard a real registration collision. The source-supported correction is to stop equating an anonymous RegisterHotKey collision with a documented Windows-owned shortcut and to present an accurate external-owner warning.
initial_investigation: Read the complete issue and all four comments, including the current-build retest and historical shortcut explanation.
Inspected runner HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflict, HasConflictWithSystemHotkey, AddHotkey, and conflict JSON serialization.
Inspected Settings GlobalHotkeyConflictManager and conflict-view consumption.
Reviewed cross-reference #50402 and found a separate attribution case rather than a direct duplicate.
Focused source review covered upstream main 71340eed47f7cf6f53b68b86a7939ad1240c3de7.

design.root_cause: The runner uses RegisterHotKey failure as an owner-blind collision probe. ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED is stored in sysConflictHotkeyMap and serialized as a System conflict, so Settings tells users a chord belongs to Windows even when the owner may be another application or a legacy reservation.
evidence: [Observed] Win+Shift+C still invokes Color Picker on the affected Windows 11 build while Settings reports a system conflict.
[Observed] HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey returns true for ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED and cannot identify the owner.
[Observed] AddHotkey inserts that result into sysConflictHotkeyMap, and GetHotkeyConflictsAsJson serializes it as sysConflicts.
[Inferred] The documentation link is misleading because the probe establishes collision, not documented Windows ownership.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: A failed RegisterHotKey probe with ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED becomes SystemConflict even though the API does not return an owner.
implementation_steps.change: Introduce explicit unknown-external registration provenance and retain SystemConflict only when ownership is known from a maintained source. Store the probing error and chord without inventing an owner.
edge_cases: Keep self-conflict and in-app conflict precedence unchanged.
tests: Known in-app collisions retain module identities.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: All owner-blind registration collisions are emitted under sysConflicts with moduleName System.
implementation_steps.change: Serialize conflict provenance explicitly so Settings can distinguish known PowerToys ownership, known system ownership if available, and unknown external ownership.
edge_cases: Do not expose process-private owner details.
Avoid converting an unknown external collision into no conflict.
tests: JSON contains the correct ownerKind for each conflict source.
Existing in-app conflict JSON remains stable.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: The UI presents sysConflicts as System and directs the user to generic Windows shortcut documentation.
implementation_steps.change: Render unknown external ownership as 'Windows or another application is already using this shortcut' and omit the system-shortcut documentation assertion. Keep module names for known in-app conflicts.
edge_cases: Accessibility name includes the exact chord and uncertainty.
tests: UI model text for unknown external, system, and in-app conflicts.
Win+Shift+C scenario no longer claims a documented Windows shortcut.

verify: Run runner hotkey-conflict unit tests or add focused tests around an injectable RegisterHotKey probe.
Manually verify free, in-app, and externally registered chords on Windows 11.
risks: Changing serialized conflict categories requires compatible Settings parsing.
Overly vague wording could reduce the usefulness of genuine system conflicts.
alternatives: Suppress Win+Shift+C specifically; rejected because the current machine may have a real external registration.
Keep calling every collision a system shortcut; rejected because RegisterHotKey does not identify the owner.

adversary.verdict: No blocking objection to the conditional catalog design; exact entry and version policy must be confirmed.
adversary.notes: Do not implement a Color Picker-only suppression.
